lab_title: AR Lab: Vectors and 2D Projectile Motion (Magnitude, Direction, Decomposition)
top_level_objectives: Represent physical quantities with vectors (magnitude and direction) and interpret them visually in AR.
Perform vector addition (tip-to-tail) and connect resultant magnitude/direction to components.
Decompose a vector into x- and y-components and relate components to the vector’s magnitude and direction via trigonometry.
Apply vector decomposition to projectile motion: identify horizontal constant velocity and vertical uniformly accelerated motion.
Use changes in launch speed and angle to predict/observe how range, flight time, and maximum height respond.

scenes.scene_name: Vectors in AR: Magnitude and Direction
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce how an initial velocity (and other quantities) can be visualized as an arrow, emphasizing that direction matters as much as magnitude.
key_visuals: A large draggable arrow representing a chosen vector in the AR space
A highlighted arc showing the vector’s direction angle from a reference axis
A grid/axis overlay with labeled +x (right) and +y (up)
A numeric readout for vector magnitude and the angle θ
student_actions: Place or select a test vector, then rotate/drag it to change its direction.
Increase/decrease the vector magnitude slider/handle and observe how the arrow length changes while the angle stays fixed.
Answer quick prompts: “What changes and what stays the same when only θ changes?”

scenes.scene_name: Tip-to-Tail Vector Addition: Resultant from Components
scenes.brief_purpose: Help students build the resultant by adding vectors geometrically and connect that resultant to what components would predict.
key_visuals: Two colored arrows (Vector A and Vector B) that can be moved
A snapping “tip-to-tail” guide showing the correct placement
A resultant arrow (R) that appears when vectors are aligned tip-to-tail
Optional dashed right-triangle illustrating the relationship between orthogonal components
student_actions: Move Vector B so its tail attaches to the tip of Vector A (tip-to-tail).
Trigger/confirm the resultant and compare its direction to the direction angle of R.
Reflect prompt: “How does changing A or B affect both the magnitude and direction of R?”

scenes.scene_name: Vector Decomposition into x and y Components
scenes.brief_purpose: Transition from abstract vector addition to expressing a single vector as orthogonal components along chosen axes.
key_visuals: A single adjustable arrow (the velocity vector) in the x–y plane
Perpendicular projection lines dropping to the x-axis and y-axis
Two component arrows (Vx along +/−x and Vy along +/−y) with labels and signs
A right-triangle diagram linking magnitude V, components Vx/Vy, and angle θ
student_actions: Choose an axis convention (horizontal x and vertical y) and request a decomposition.
Rotate the original vector to new angles; observe how Vx and Vy change while the original arrow stays the same.
Use the on-screen triangle to verify trigonometric relationships (e.g., Vx = V cosθ, Vy = V sinθ) with student-entered predicted values.

scenes.scene_name: Projectile Decomposition: Horizontal vs Vertical Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply vector decomposition to physics: show that vx stays constant (no horizontal acceleration) while vy changes due to gravity.
key_visuals: A projectile launch setup at a chosen point with an initial velocity vector arrow at angle θ
A horizontal velocity component arrow that remains the same length/direction during flight (indicator/track)
A vertical component arrow that changes over time, labeled with “upward” vs “downward” direction
A gravity vector or acceleration marker pointing downward (ay = −g)
A split-screen or togglable overlay showing x(t) as linear and y(t) as curved/quadratic
student_actions: Launch the projectile and observe the separate “horizontal” and “vertical” indicators.
Pause at multiple time stamps; for each, state whether vx and vy are increasing/decreasing/constant.
Predict: “If I double the launch angle but keep speed the same, what should happen to vx and vy?”

scenes.scene_name: Trajectory Emergence: Combine Constant vx and Accelerated vy
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how the parabolic path results from combining independent motions in x and y (independence insight).
key_visuals: A visible 2D trajectory trace (parabolic curve) behind the moving projectile
A ghosted horizontal motion marker showing equal time steps along x
A vertical position marker updating with uniform acceleration
A composite reconstruction view: at each time step, the projectile’s location is built from the x-position and y-position pieces
Overlay of equations as conceptual anchors (constant vx; y accelerated under g) without heavy computation
student_actions: Enable the “reconstruction” to see how the projectile’s position is assembled each frame.
Compare two different launches that share the same vx but differ in vy; observe how the trajectory shapes differ.
Answer: “Which feature controls the curvature of the path?” focusing on vertical acceleration.

scenes.scene_name: Parameter Study: Changing Launch Angle and Speed
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding by exploring how launch angle and speed affect range, time of flight, and maximum height.
key_visuals: Controls for launch speed v0 and launch angle θ with immediate AR updates
Multiple trajectory overlays (e.g., faint previous shots) for comparison
Markers for apex height, landing point, and total range
Readouts for maximum height, horizontal range, and estimated flight time
A vector/triangle indicator showing the decomposed components for each shot (Vx, Vy)
student_actions: Run a small set of trials (e.g., three angles with the same speed) and record observed changes to range and max height.
Run trials varying speed at a fixed angle; identify which outcomes scale more strongly with v0 (noting horizontal vs vertical contributions).
Challenge prompt: “Choose a target range (or target height) and adjust θ and/or v0 to hit it; explain using Vx and Vy.”
